guides.title: How Long Do Running Shoes Last? Miles, Signs, and the Foam
guides.excerpt: The 300 to 500 mile rule is a rough range, not a deadline. Your body and the shoe itself give better signals than the odometer does.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
Every runner has heard "replace your shoes every 300 to 500 miles." That's a range with a wide gap in the middle, and it's built on average shoes, average runners and average roads. You'll get a better read from the shoe in your hand.

## The mileage range depends on the shoe and on you

The range exists because foam, outsole rubber and body weight all vary. A heavier runner compresses the midsole more each stride. A runner who lands softly on trails wears an outsole differently from someone who scuffs a heel on pavement.

Plenty of daily trainers, like the [Pegasus 42](/shoes/nike-pegasus-42), list durability as a strength in our data, with notes on durable outsoles and suitability for high mileage. Plated race shoes, as a rule, don't last as long. I'd treat 300 as an early check and 500 as the point where you stop asking questions and replace.

The evidence behind the exact numbers is thin. Lab tests show midsole foam loses some of its cushioning over time, but how much that matters to a runner is harder to measure. Nobody can hand you a mileage that's right for your body.

## The signs that beat the odometer

Look at the shoe first. Press your thumb into the midsole. If it feels dead and creased, with deep wrinkles running across the foam, it has lost its bounce. Check the outsole too. When the rubber is worn through to the foam at the heel or ball of the foot, grip and protection are gone.

Then check the upper. A heel counter that has collapsed or a toe box that has torn out lets your foot slide around, and that's worth fixing before the cushioning is.

Now check yourself. If your legs feel more beaten up after easy runs than they used to, and the shoe is past 300 miles, that's a reasonable hint it's time. It isn't proof. A hard training block or poor sleep can do the same. If a pain keeps showing up or gets worse, that's a conversation for a doctor or physical therapist, not a shoe swap.

Here's a simple trick I use. Keep a spare pair that's newer, and do an easy run in each on back-to-back days. If the old pair feels flat by comparison, you have your answer.

## Softer foam usually wears out sooner

Firm shoes feel the same on day 1 and day 300. Soft ones feel different, since the foam is what gives them the ride. That's why the budget [Winflo 12](/shoes/nike-winflo-12), a firmer trainer with a durable outsole, ages gracefully. A plush shoe like the [Hoka Clifton 11](/shoes/hoka-clifton-11) has a 42mm stack of soft EVA and gives you more of a before and after.

Neither is wrong. If you love a bouncy shoe, expect to replace it a little earlier than a firm one.

## Rotating pairs stretches the life of both

Foam needs time to recover between runs. Alternating two pairs lets each one rebound, and in my experience both last longer. A 2015 study followed 264 recreational runners for 22 weeks and found those who used more than one pair had a lower risk of running-related injury. It was observational, so it can't prove the rotation caused it. Still, it's a good reason to try it, and our [guide to rotating two pairs](/rundown/shoe-rotation-two-pairs) shows how.

Log your miles on whatever app you use and set an alert at 300. When it goes off, run the thumb test and check the outsole. If the shoe still passes, keep going.

If you want your next pair to last, the [shoe selector](/tools/shoe-selector) lets you filter for durable daily trainers.

Write the start date inside the tongue of each pair, and you'll never have to guess.

guides.title: How Many Gels for a Marathon? The Math by Finish Time
guides.excerpt: Plan on 60 grams of carbs an hour, which is roughly three gels per hour at 20 grams each. For a four-hour marathon that adds up to about 10 or 11 gels, and you have to practice it.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
The honest answer to "how many gels" is a number of grams, not a number of gels. Gels differ, so the useful math starts with carbs per hour and works backward to the packet count.

## Start from carbs per hour, not from the gel

A 2014 review by Asker Jeukendrup in Sports Medicine laid out targets by duration. For events lasting about two to three hours, it recommends around 60 grams of carbohydrate per hour, and for ultra-endurance efforts about 90. The older American College of Sports Medicine guidance was 30 to 60 grams an hour, and a later consensus statement stretched the range to 30 to 90.

Notice that these are guidelines for athletes in general, and the review itself says the numbers depend on the type and duration of activity. For a marathon, 60 grams an hour is a sensible target for most people who can tolerate it. Slower runners who spend four or more hours out there can reasonably aim a bit higher.

The 90 gram figure relies on mixing glucose and fructose, which the body absorbs through different routes. If you're new to fueling, treat 90 as something to build toward, not where you start.

## Then work backward to gels

Most gels carry somewhere around 20 to 25 grams of carbohydrate per packet, and the label tells you exactly. Check yours, because the number varies by brand and by whether it's a thin gel or a thick one. Our own fuel database doesn't have clean carb counts for every product yet, so I won't pretend to quote one.

At 60 grams an hour and 20 grams a gel, you're taking one gel every 20 minutes. Here's what that comes to across finish times:

- A 3:30 marathon takes about 10 gels, with a few fewer if you start fueling at mile 4
- A 4:00 marathon works out to 11 to 12 gels
- A 5:00 marathon runs 14 or so, which is when chews or drink mix start to help with the monotony

Subtract anything you take in sports drink at aid stations, since those carbs count too. If the course drink has 20 grams per bottle and you finish one an hour, you can skip a gel.

## Start early and stay steady

Take your first gel around 30 to 45 minutes in, well before you feel hungry. By the time you feel flat at mile 20, you've waited too long, and I've done exactly that. Small and regular beats big and late.

Water goes with the gel. Take it at an aid station, sip, and wash it down. Gels without water are a common stomach problem, and [race-day fueling mistakes](/rundown/race-day-fueling-mistakes) has the full list of ways this goes sideways.

## Your stomach decides the ceiling

Here's where plans meet the real world. Most runners can build up to 60 grams an hour, but only by practicing it in training. If you've never taken more than one gel on a long run, don't try 11 on race day.

Our guide to [training your gut for race fueling](/rundown/train-your-gut-race-fueling) lays out a progression. The short version is to add a gel to each long run until your whole race plan feels boring.

The [fueling tool](/tools/fueling) turns your finish time and race into a schedule, so you can see the timing before you open a single packet.

This plan is wrong for you if you're running a 10K or a fast half, where under 75 minutes usually needs little beyond water. It's also not a medical plan. If you have diabetes or another health condition that affects how you handle carbohydrates, talk to your doctor or a dietitian before you adopt a fueling target.

Pick a gel you can stomach, write the gel times on your arm or in your watch, and rehearse the whole thing on your next long run.

guides.title: How to Find Your Running Cadence and Pick Songs to Match
guides.excerpt: Count your steps for 30 seconds, double it, and you have your cadence. Then change it by a few percent at most, and let music do the nudging.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
You don't need a watch to learn your cadence. You need 30 seconds, a flat stretch of road and a way to count. Once you have the number, it tells you which songs will feel natural and which will fight you.

## Counting steps for 30 seconds gives you the number

Warm up for ten minutes at your normal easy pace. Then pick a stretch where you can run steadily and count how many times your right foot lands in 30 seconds. Multiply by four. That's your steps per minute, which is what everyone means by cadence.

Do it a few times on different days, and at different paces. You'll notice it climbs as you speed up. A runner at an easy pace might sit in the 160s and hit the 170s or 180s on a tempo run. Those are ballpark numbers, not targets, and plenty of good runners fall outside them.

Most running watches report cadence too. If yours does, check it against your hand count once so you know it's reading steps and not strides.

## You almost never need to change it by much

Here's the useful research. A 2011 study from Heiderscheit's lab at the University of Wisconsin put 45 recreational runners on a treadmill at their normal step rate and at plus and minus 5 and 10 percent. Raising step rate by 5 percent cut the energy the knee absorbed, and a 10 percent rise reduced it at the hip too. The authors also noted that a big change from your natural rate may be hard to hold and could cost you speed.

That's one lab study on healthy runners at a fixed speed. It doesn't prove a magic number, and it isn't a reason to chase 180. If your natural cadence is 158, a target of 166 is a reasonable experiment. A target of 180 is a different way of running.

If something hurts when you run, that's a question for a clinician or a physical therapist, not a cadence app.

## Match songs to your cadence, then go easy on the beat

The point of matching music is that a song at your cadence feels like it's running with you. A track at 165 BPM suits a runner at 165 steps a minute. That's why a playlist built for your pace works better than a random shuffle.

The [Music Finder](/tools/music) builds playlists around a BPM or pace you pick, so you can start with your counted number and see what comes up.

Half-time songs are the trick most runners miss. A track at 85 BPM can match 170 steps a minute if you land one foot on every beat and the other between. It means you aren't limited to the fast end of the catalog.

## To nudge your cadence, use songs a few BPM above your own

Pick a song 3 to 5 percent above your natural rate and run to it for a couple of minutes at the end of an easy run. Don't force it for the whole workout. If the beat feels like a leash, drop back to your own rhythm.

Do that once or twice a week and your body will drift toward the new number without you thinking about it. Faster isn't automatically better, and your stride length will shorten a little as cadence rises. That's the trade, and it's the reason I'd keep changes small.

If you also rotate shoes, the heel drop and foam can change how your cadence feels. Our [two-shoe rotation guide](/rundown/shoe-rotation-two-pairs) covers that overlap.

If you're picking a pair for faster, higher-cadence days, the [shoe selector](/tools/shoe-selector) can filter by usage.

Count your 30 seconds tomorrow, write the number on your phone, and build one playlist around it.

guides.title: Best Running Shoes for Beginners: Pick for Fit, Not Specs
guides.excerpt: Your first pair should be a neutral, moderately cushioned trainer that fits the day you try it on. The Ghost 18 is our default at $150, with the Winflo 12 at $110 as the cheaper way in.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
Most first-time buyers open a spec sheet and start comparing stack heights. That's backwards. Between two sensible trainers, the one that doesn't pinch your toes will beat the one with the better numbers every time, because you'll actually run in it.

Here's how I'd shop, and the three shoes I'd start with.

## Fit decides it, and the specs mostly don't

Nearly every shoe in the beginner tier sits in the same narrow band. The [Ghost 18](/shoes/brooks-ghost-18) has a 36mm stack and a 12mm drop. The [Pegasus 42](/shoes/nike-pegasus-42) is 37mm and 10mm. A two-millimeter stack gap isn't something a new runner will feel, so don't let it make the call.

What you will feel is the first mile. Your toes should have a thumb's width of room in front, your heel shouldn't slip, and nothing should rub. If a shoe feels almost right in the store, it will feel wrong by mile four. Try them on in the afternoon, when your feet are a little bigger, and wear the socks you'll run in.

One more thing about fit: skip the shoe that was great for your friend. Feet differ more than shoe models do.

## The Ghost 18 is the safe first pair

At $150 and 9.8 oz, the Brooks Ghost 18 is the shoe I'd point most new runners to. It's a neutral trainer with moderate cushioning, and our data lists the pros as a dependable ride for every easy run, a fit that suits most feet, and wide sizes. The outsole is durable, so your first pair won't wear out early.

The catch is that it plays it safe. It has little energy return and feels firmer than the max-cushion shoes. If you want something that feels exciting, this isn't it. If you want something you'll forget about while you run, it is.

It's the wrong pick if you know you have a narrow heel that lifts out of most shoes, or if you want a soft, pillowy ride. For that, look below.

## The cheaper way in, and the softer one

If $150 is a stretch, the [Winflo 12](/shoes/nike-winflo-12) runs $110 and weighs 9.7 oz. It's firmer than Nike's premium foams and it's not built for workouts, but it's a comfortable, durable everyday shoe. For a runner doing three easy runs a week, that's the whole job. We cover more of this price tier in [our under-$120 guide](/rundown/good-running-shoes-under-120).

If you want a softer ride, the [Hoka Clifton 11](/shoes/hoka-clifton-11) is $150 with a 42mm stack and an 8mm drop. It's the plush option and it works for walking and standing all day, which suits a lot of beginners. The honest downside is that it's not versatile at faster paces, and the foam is ordinary EVA for the money. Think of it as an easy-day shoe that happens to be a fine first shoe.

## What to ignore on your first pair

Skip the carbon-plated racers. They're built for race day and they cost more than a beginner needs. If you're curious about them later, [how to choose your first racing shoe](/rundown/how-to-choose-your-first-racing-shoe) covers when they make sense.

Skip stability shoes unless a running store or a clinician has a reason to put you in one. Support is a decision, not a default. And don't chase the lightest shoe, because the 9.7 to 9.8 oz range is plenty light for easy miles.

Don't overthink the first month either. A good-fitting neutral trainer will carry you through your first 5K, your first 10K, and the weeks of figuring out what you like. By then you'll have opinions, and your second pair will be a better-informed purchase than your first.

If you'd rather filter by your own foot and budget, the [shoe selector](/tools/shoe-selector) narrows the list in a couple of minutes. Otherwise, try on the Ghost, try on the Clifton, and buy the one your feet forget about.

guides.title: Good Running Shoes Under $120: What You Give Up, What You Don't
guides.excerpt: The $150-and-up default is a marketing achievement, not a biomechanical fact. Here's what cheaper shoes actually cost you, and the five worth buying right now.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
The average price of the ten most popular daily trainers in our database is about $150. None of them will make you meaningfully healthier than the shoes one shelf down. The budget tier is where brands quietly sell last year's ideas at honest prices, and for most training miles that's exactly what you want.

Here's the deal you're actually making, followed by the shoes worth your money.

## What you give up under $120

Mostly, you give up the newest foams. Budget midsoles are typically firmer EVA blends — durable and predictable, but without the bounce that makes a $170 trainer feel like it's helping. You'll notice it most late in long runs, when softer, lighter foam stops feeling like a luxury.

What you don't reliably give up is weight — the $110 [Winflo 12](/shoes/nike-winflo-12) is 9.7 oz, and the $145 Pegasus 42 is 9.8. What you do give up is race-day snap; there are no plates down here, and there shouldn't be.

## What you don't give up

Fit, durability, and injury protection. Budget uppers are sometimes better than premium ones — simpler mesh, fewer clever ideas to rub you wrong. Firmer foams often outlast soft superfoams by hundreds of miles. And no study has ever shown expensive shoes reduce injury risk; comfort and consistency matter, price doesn't.

## The five worth buying

- **Default pick: [Nike Winflo 12](/shoes/nike-winflo-12), $110.** The boring, correct answer. Moderate cushion, 10mm drop, wide availability, and nothing about it needs an apology. If you're not sure what you want, this.
- **If you overpronate: [ASICS GT-1000 15](/shoes/asics-gt-1000-15), $100.** Real structured support at a hundred dollars — the cheapest legitimate stability trainer we track, and the pick if your old shoes wear hard on the inner edge.
- **If you want fast-day energy: [Saucony Kinvara 15](/shoes/saucony-kinvara-15), $120.** At 7.2 oz it's lighter than most $180 shoes. The catch is a firm ride and a 4mm drop that loads your calves — ease in if you're coming from 10mm.
- **If it's between shoes and groceries: [New Balance Fresh Foam 680 v9](/shoes/new-balance-fresh-foam-680-v9), $85.** A genuinely decent trainer, not a treadmill-and-errands shoe. The [Nike Revolution 8](/shoes/nike-revolution-8) at $70 exists one rung below it, and that rung is noticeable.
- **If you like a firmer, quicker feel every day: [Brooks Launch 12](/shoes/brooks-launch-12), $115.** Less pillow, more pop, 8.5 oz. The pick for runners who find the Winflo dull.

Prices are current list from our database; all five are frequently on sale below these numbers, at which point this whole tier becomes absurd value.

## When paying more is right

Spend up when you're past roughly 35 miles a week (softer foam earns its keep on tired legs), when you've found a specific fit nothing cheap matches, or when you're buying a second, faster shoe to go with a budget daily — a [rotation of two](/rundown/shoe-rotation-two-pairs) built around one $110 shoe and one $150 shoe beats a single $260 shoe doing everything badly.

If you want a pick matched to your feet and week instead of a list, the [shoe finder](/tools/shoe-selector) narrows our full [database](/shoes) to three shoes with the tradeoffs stated. It won't care what anything costs unless you tell it to.

guides.title: Your Gut Is Trainable: How to Practice Race Fueling Before It Counts
guides.excerpt: The runners who take gels at mile 18 without drama practiced it for months. Gut training is real, it's boring, and it's the cheapest fitness you'll ever buy.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
Every marathon has a stretch after mile 16 where you can watch fueling plans die. Runners slowing to walk through aid stations, hands on knees, doing math about porta-potties. Most of them made the same bet: that a stomach which had never handled 60 grams of carbs an hour at race effort would figure it out on the day.

It won't. But it can learn, and the learning is straightforward.

## What gut training actually changes

Your intestines adapt to what you ask of them. Feed them carbohydrate during running consistently and they upregulate the transporters that move sugar out of your gut and into your blood — which means more energy absorbed and less sitting in your stomach causing trouble. Sports-science labs have measured this repeatedly: a few weeks of practicing in-run fueling measurably increases carb absorption and cuts GI complaints.

The adaptation is specific, though. Handling a gel on a casual Saturday run says little about handling one at marathon effort in month-three heat, because hard running diverts blood away from your gut exactly when you're asking it to work. You have to practice under something like race conditions.

## The progression

Give it six to eight weeks. It slots into the long runs you're already doing.

- Weeks 1–2: take fuel on every run over 75 minutes, aiming for 30–40 grams of carbs per hour. One gel every 40 minutes gets you there. It'll feel like too much. That's the point of starting now.
- Weeks 3–4: raise it to 50–60 grams per hour, and take at least one gel during the harder segments of a workout, not just the easy miles.
- Weeks 5 onward: hold 60 grams per hour on every long run. Going past 75 toward 90 — worthwhile for marathons over 3:30 — needs products mixing glucose and fructose, because the two sugars use separate absorption pathways. Most current gels do this; the label will say maltodextrin and fructose.

Two rules make the practice transfer. Use the exact products, flavors, and caffeine doses you'll race with — your race-morning stomach is not the place to discover you hate salted watermelon. And practice the logistics too: carrying the gels, opening one at pace with numb fingers, washing it down with water rather than sports drink so you don't stack sugar on sugar.

## When it goes wrong

A bad session is data. Sloshing usually means too much volume at once — smaller, more frequent doses. Cramping or urgency often traces to a high-caffeine gel or to fructose-heavy fuel before your gut adapted; drop to glucose-primary products for two weeks and rebuild. Nausea at hard effort mostly means you took fuel too late and were already deep in deficit — earlier, smaller, more often is the fix for almost everything.

What you're looking for by taper time is boredom. Fueling at 60 grams an hour should feel like brushing your teeth.

## Turn it into a schedule

The [fuel planner](/tools/fueling) does the arithmetic for you: give it your distance, expected time, and conditions and it produces a minute-by-minute schedule and a packing list you can rehearse on your next long run. And if you want the companion piece — the race-day errors that undo months of good practice — we wrote up the [five fueling mistakes that wreck marathons](/rundown/race-day-fueling-mistakes).

Your legs get months of training before race day. Give your gut a few weeks of the same.

guides.title: Two Pairs Is a Rotation: A Sane Guide to Rotating Running Shoes
guides.excerpt: Shoe rotation gets sold as a five-shoe collection project. It isn't. Here's the two-pair version that covers almost everyone, and the honest case for a third.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
Somewhere along the way, "rotate your shoes" turned into "own a shoe wardrobe." Shoe content loves the five-slot rotation: the daily, the max-cushion recovery shoe, the tempo shoe, the race shoe, the trail shoe. That's a fun collection. It is not a requirement for running well.

Two pairs cover almost everyone. Here's how to think about it.

## Why rotate at all

Two reasons hold up.

The first is mechanical variety. Different shoes load your legs differently — a 4mm drop shifts work toward the calf and Achilles, a 10mm drop shifts it away; a firm shoe lets your foot do more stabilizing than a soft one. Alternating shoes spreads repetitive stress around instead of drilling the identical pattern into the same tissue every day. A 2015 Luxembourg study of 264 runners found that people who rotated multiple pairs had a 39% lower injury rate than single-shoe runners. It's observational — runners who buy more shoes may differ in a dozen other ways — so treat it as a hint, not a law. But the mechanism is plausible and the cost of acting on it is low.

The second is that foam needs time. EVA and the newer superfoams compress on every footstrike and rebound slowly. Give a midsole a day off and you're running on the shoe as designed, not on yesterday's flattened version of it.

## The two-pair core

**Pair one: a daily trainer you'd trust with 80% of your miles.** Durable, comfortable at easy pace, stable enough that your form doesn't fall apart when you're tired. This is where the boring choice wins — there's a reason the [Brooks Ghost 17](/shoes/brooks-ghost-17) ($150), the [Nike Pegasus 41](/shoes/nike-pegasus-41) ($140), and the [Hoka Clifton 10](/shoes/hoka-clifton-10) ($150) sit at the top of our popularity data year after year.

**Pair two: something lighter that makes fast days feel different.** Not necessarily a carbon plate. A lightweight trainer with a livelier foam — the [Hoka Mach 6](/shoes/hoka-mach-6) at $140 or the [Adidas Adizero Evo SL](/shoes/adidas-adizero-evo-sl) at $150 — changes your turnover, your contact feel, and your enthusiasm for intervals. The mechanical-variety benefit comes free with it.

That's the rotation. Daily shoe most days, fast shoe on quality days, and neither midsole ever runs on back-to-back days if you're running quality twice a week.

## When a third pair earns its place

- You're marathon training with a race under three months away and you want a plated race shoe. Fine — but the [Vaporfly 4](/shoes/nike-vaporfly-4) is $260, and it's a worse daily trainer than shoes at half the price. Buy it as a race tool, practice in it twice, save the rest.
- Your daily trainer is past 300 miles and you've started the replacement early. Overlapping old and new is quietly the most useful rotation there is.
- You genuinely run trails. Road shoes on wet roots is how ankles have bad days.

Notice what's not on the list: a dedicated recovery shoe. If your daily trainer isn't comfortable on your easiest days, you bought the wrong daily trainer.

## Matching pairs to your actual week

The math only works if the second shoe gets used. Running four days a week, all easy? One good pair and an early-overlap replacement beats two half-used shoes aging in a closet — foam degrades with time, not just miles.

If you want picks matched to your own week, budget, and feet instead of ours, the [shoe finder](/tools/shoe-selector) asks three questions and gives you three shoes with the tradeoffs stated. Or browse everything we track in the [shoe database](/shoes).

Start with two. Let the third pair earn its way in.

guides.title: A Substitute Teacher and a 45-Year-Old Mom Just Won the LA Marathon
guides.excerpt: Nathan Martin coaches high school track in Michigan. Priscah Cherono is a 45-year-old mother of three running her second marathon ever. On Sunday, they both won the LA Marathon, and neither victory was supposed to happen.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
The 2026 Los Angeles Marathon was supposed to be a straightforward race. It was anything but. When the dust settled on Sunday, a high school substitute teacher from Michigan and a 45-year-old Kenyan mother of three stood at the top of the podium. Two of the most unlikely champions in the race's 41-year history.

## Nathan Martin: The Coach Who Outran Everyone

Nathan Martin, 36, is a substitute teacher and cross-country coach at Jackson High School in Michigan. He is not sponsored by a major shoe brand. He does not have a professional training group. He picks up shifts at a high school to pay the bills between races.

None of that mattered on Sunday.

Martin entered the race as a relative unknown to casual fans, but he's no beginner. He's a three-time U.S. Olympic Trials qualifier and holds the record as the fastest U.S.-born Black marathoner, with a 2:10:45 personal best set at the 2023 Grandma's Marathon.

Still, he wasn't the favorite. Kenya's Michael Kimani Kamau held the lead for most of the race and looked like the winner heading into the final stretch. Then everything changed.

### The Closest Finish in LA Marathon History

With 300 meters to go, Kamau briefly followed the race motorcade off the marked path, ducking behind a spectator waving a Kenyan flag before jumping back on course. The detour lasted roughly five seconds, an eternity in a race decided by hundredths.

Martin, running from way back, was closing fast. At the finish line, Kamau collapsed and dove forward as Martin surged past. The official time difference: 0.01 seconds. Martin crossed in 2:11:16.50. Kamau was taken away on a stretcher after reportedly skipping fluids throughout the race.

It was the closest finish in LA Marathon history, shattering the previous record of 0.07 seconds set in 2019. Martin became the first African-American man to win the race in its 41 years.

## Priscah Cherono: The Mom Who Beat Everybody

If Martin's win was dramatic, Cherono's was dominant.

Priscah Cherono is 45 years old. She is a mother of three. This was her second professional marathon. Ever.

She led from Mile 1 to Mile 26.2. Nobody challenged her. She crossed the finish line in 2:25:18.31, more than two minutes ahead of American Kellyn Taylor in second.

But here's the part that makes it truly remarkable: the LA Marathon uses a "Marathon Chase" format where elite women start 15 minutes and 45 seconds ahead of the elite men. The first person to physically cross the finish line, regardless of gender, wins a $10,000 bonus.

Cherono won it. She crossed the line before any of the men, including Martin, despite them chasing her with nearly a 16-minute head start. A 45-year-old woman in her second marathon outran every man on the course to the tape.

### From the Olympics to Motherhood to the Marathon

Cherono is not a complete unknown in the running world. She represented Kenya in the 5,000 meters at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. But that was 18 years ago. She stepped away from competitive running, had three children and only recently shifted to the marathon distance at age 45.

Most elite marathoners peak in their late 20s or early 30s. Cherono is rewriting that timeline entirely.

## What This Means for the Sport

Both victories share a common thread: these are people who refused to fit the mold of what a marathon champion is supposed to look like.

Martin is a public school teacher who coaches teenagers during the week and races on weekends. Cherono is a 45-year-old mother who came out of an 18-year competitive hiatus to dominate a major marathon.

In a sport increasingly defined by super shoes, altitude camps and six-figure sponsorship deals, the 2026 LA Marathon was a reminder that the marathon doesn't care about your resume. It only cares about who crosses the line first.

And on Sunday in Los Angeles, it was a substitute teacher from Jackson, Michigan, and a mom from Kenya.

guides.title: How to Choose Your First Racing Shoe
guides.excerpt: Carbon-plated super shoes are everywhere, but are they right for you? Here's what to consider before dropping $250 on race-day footwear.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
Carbon-plated super shoes have taken over the racing world. Every major brand now has at least one, and the technology keeps getting faster. But if you're buying your first dedicated racing shoe, the options can feel overwhelming.

## Do You Actually Need a Racing Shoe?

If you're running a half marathon or marathon and care about your finishing time, a racing shoe can genuinely help. Studies show carbon-plated shoes improve running economy by 2–4%, which translates to roughly 1–3 minutes over a marathon.

But if you're running your first race and just want to finish comfortably, your daily trainer is probably fine. Racing shoes are built for speed, not comfort over untrained legs.

## What Makes a Racing Shoe Different

Racing shoes share three key features:

- A carbon fiber or composite plate embedded in the midsole that acts as a lever during toe-off
- Lightweight, high-energy-return foam (usually PEBA-based) that bounces back more energy than traditional EVA
- Aggressive rocker geometry that rolls you forward through your stride

The trade-off: they're less stable, less durable and more expensive than daily trainers. Most racing shoes last 100–150 miles before the foam loses its pop.

## How to Pick the Right One

### Match it to your race distance
For a 5K or 10K, you want something lighter and more responsive. For a marathon, prioritize cushion and energy return. Your legs need help at mile 22, not mile 2.

### Consider your body weight
Heavier runners (180+ lbs) may want shoes with more foam and a stiffer plate. Lighter runners can get away with minimal designs that prioritize ground feel.

### Try before you race
Never debut a racing shoe on race day. Do at least 2–3 tempo or long runs in them first to make sure your feet, ankles and calves can handle the different mechanics.

## Our Top Picks for First-Time Racers

- Saucony Endorphin Speed: Not a full carbon plate (nylon), which makes it more forgiving and versatile. Great as a first fast shoe.
- Nike Vaporfly: The original super shoe. Proven, reliable and widely available.
- Adidas Adizero Adios Pro: Excellent energy return with a unique rod-based plate system.
- Hoka Rocket X: Softer feel with good stability for a plated shoe.

## The Bottom Line

A racing shoe is a tool, not a magic bullet. It won't fix bad training, but it can give well-prepared runners a meaningful edge. Start with something forgiving like the Endorphin Speed, save the full carbon plates for when you know what you want.

guides.title: 5 Race-Day Fueling Mistakes That Will Wreck Your Marathon
guides.excerpt: Most bonks and GI disasters are completely preventable. Here are the mistakes we see over and over, and how to avoid them.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
You trained for 16 weeks. Your legs are ready. But race day still goes sideways because of what you ate (or didn't eat) during the run. Here are the five fueling mistakes that ruin more marathons than undertrained legs.

## 1. Trying Something New on Race Day

This is the golden rule of race nutrition, and people still break it constantly. That free gel at mile 8? Skip it if you've never tried that brand. The sports drink on course? It might not be what your stomach expects.

Practice your exact fueling plan during at least 3–4 long training runs before the race.

## 2. Starting Fueling Too Late

By the time you feel hungry or low on energy, you're already behind. Glycogen depletion is a slow process, and gels take 15–20 minutes to hit your bloodstream.

Start taking in carbs by mile 4–5 of a marathon. Aim for 60–90g of carbs per hour for efforts over 2 hours.

## 3. Not Drinking Enough Water With Gels

Gels are concentrated carbohydrate. Without water, they sit in your stomach and cause cramping, nausea or worse. Every gel should be followed by 4–6 oz of water.

Conversely, don't wash gels down with sports drink. That's a double dose of sugar that can overwhelm your gut.

## 4. Ignoring Sodium

Sweat contains sodium, and as you lose it, your muscles lose their ability to contract efficiently. This is a major cause of late-race cramping.

Aim for 300–700mg of sodium per hour, depending on your sweat rate and conditions. Salt tabs, electrolyte drinks or salty snacks all work.

## 5. Going Out Too Fast and Burning Through Glycogen

This is a fueling mistake disguised as a pacing mistake. Running the first half too fast burns glycogen at a dramatically higher rate, which means you'll deplete your stores before mile 20 no matter how many gels you take.

Stick to your goal pace from the start. Negative splits are always better than positive ones.

## Build Your Plan

Use our Fueling Planner to build a mile-by-mile nutrition schedule based on your goal time, body weight and race conditions. It's free and takes about 30 seconds.

guides.title: Spring 2026 Shoe Releases Worth Watching
guides.excerpt: From the Saucony Endorphin Speed 6 to the Brooks Ghost Max 4, the best new running shoes dropping this spring.
guides.author: Runner Toolkit
guides.body:
Spring is prime time for running shoe releases, and 2026 is shaping up to be one of the most competitive seasons in years. Here are the shoes we're most excited about.

## Daily Trainers

### Brooks Ghost Max 4
Brooks continues to refine the Ghost Max, which has become one of the most popular max-cushion daily trainers. The v4 gets a slightly updated midsole geometry and improved upper breathability. If you liked the 3, you'll love this.

### Skechers Aero Burst 2
Skechers keeps quietly making excellent running shoes. The Aero Burst 2 features their HyperBurst+ foam and a lower price point than most competitors. Don't sleep on this one.

## Racing Shoes

### Saucony Endorphin Speed 6
The Speed line has been our go-to recommendation for runners buying their first fast shoe, and the v6 doesn't mess with the formula. Updated PWRRUN PB foam, refreshed upper, same versatile nylon plate.

### Saucony Endorphin Elite 3
For serious racers, the Elite 3 pushes Saucony's carbon plate tech further with a new full-length carbon plate and lighter overall weight. Early reviews are promising.

### Brooks Hyperion Elite 6
Brooks' race-day shoe gets a significant update with new DNA Flash foam and a redesigned carbon plate. They're clearly targeting the Vaporfly and Adios Pro crowd.

## Trail

### Brooks Cascadia Elite
A new entry in the premium trail racing space. Carbon plate in a trail shoe is still relatively uncommon, and Brooks is betting runners want that speed advantage off-road too.

### Brooks Ghost Trail 2
For trail runners who want Ghost-level comfort on dirt. Not a racing shoe. This is about comfortable miles on groomed trails.

## When They Drop

Most of these are hitting stores between March and May 2026. We'll update our Shoe Finder with full specs and recommendations as each shoe becomes available.

Check the Shoe Finder to see what's already in our database and find the right shoe for your needs.
